title: Density is not the energy of the whole packet
question: Why does a finite light complex need a volume calculation?
recap: In the new frame the light’s energy density changes by the factor q squared, while the volume of the same light complex, measured at one instant of the new time, changes by 1/q. Its total energy therefore changes by q, the same factor as its frequency.
premises: The same finite light complex is compared, each frame measuring its volume at one instant of its own time.
The waves transform as plane waves, with q defined from the light’s direction in the original frame.
limitations: A light complex is not a rod, and light has no rest frame.
The result needs neither light quanta nor the mass-energy relation it later supports.

overview.text: In the new frame the light’s energy density changes by the factor \(q^2\), while the volume of the same light complex, measured at one instant of the new time, changes by \(1/q\). Its total energy therefore changes by \(q\), the same factor as its frequency.

full.spoken: Energy density scales by q squared, packet volume by inverse q, and total energy by q.

full.text: Einstein bounds the light complex by a sphere that moves with the light. That boundary is not a body at rest in either frame, so the ordinary contraction of a material body does not apply to it. At \(0.6c\), for light travelling the same way as the observer, \(q = 0.5\): the density falls to one quarter, the volume doubles, and the total energy halves.

Treating the light complex as a body at rest in the original frame, and shrinking its volume by \(1/\gamma = 0.8\), would give a total-energy factor of \(0.25 \times 0.8 = 0.2\) instead of 0.5. For light crossing the motion at right angles in the original frame the two volume factors happen to agree, both 0.8, so that case alone cannot catch the mistake. The light-packet laboratory includes the case that tells them apart.
The mass-energy paper of September 1905 starts from exactly this transformation of light energy. It does not assume \(E = mc^2\) in advance, and it needs no localized light quanta.

full.returnCaption: Return to why a light complex needs its volume.

steps.text: Letters: in §8 the paper's light has amplitude A in K and \(A'\) in k, and \(A^2/8\pi\) is its energy per unit volume in Gaussian units; a, b, c are the direction cosines of the wave normal in K, R the radius of a sphere that moves with the light, S and \(S'\) the volumes enclosed, E and \(E'\) the energy of the light complex, and V the speed of light. This explanation writes u for the energy density, \(V_{\mathrm{packet}}\) for the volume, and q for the frequency factor \(\gamma(1-(v/c)\cos\varphi)\) of §7.

items: The density. §7 found that the amplitude changes by the same factor q as the frequency, so the energy density, which goes as the amplitude squared, changes by \(q^2\).
The paper points out that \(A'^2/A^2\) would be the ratio of the energies only if the light complex had the same volume in K and k. It does not.
A boundary around the same light: the sphere \((x-Vat)^2+(y-Vbt)^2+(z-Vct)^2=R^2\) moves with the light, so no energy crosses its surface, and it always encloses the same light complex.

The same surface seen in k at the instant τ = 0: substitute \(x=\beta ξ\) (since τ = 0 means \(t=vx/V^2\)), \(t=\beta vξ/V^2\), y = η, z = ζ. The paper prints the result, an ellipsoid: \((\beta ξ-a\beta\frac{v}{V}ξ)^2+(η-b\beta\frac{v}{V}ξ)^2+(ζ-c\beta\frac{v}{V}ξ)^2=R^2\).

Its volume. The left side is a sphere of radius R in new coordinates \(u_1=\beta(1-av/V)ξ\), \(u_2=η-b\beta(v/V)ξ\), \(u_3=ζ-c\beta(v/V)ξ\). That change of coordinates is triangular, so it multiplies volumes by the product of its diagonal, \(\beta(1-av/V)\cdot1\cdot1\).
So the ellipsoid's volume is the sphere's divided by \(\beta(1-a\,v/V)\), which is q: \(S'/S=\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}/(1-(v/V)\cos\varphi)=1/q\), as the paper prints it.
Multiply density by volume: \(q^2\times1/q=q\). Together, the three formulas below.

steps.spoken: Energy density scales by q squared, packet volume by inverse q, and total energy by q.

items: The paper's result, printed as \(E'/E=(1-\frac{v}{V}\cos\varphi)/\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\), becomes \(\sqrt{(1-v/V)/(1+v/V)}\) for φ = 0. It remarks that the energy and the frequency of a light complex change with the observer's motion by the same law.
Worked at 0.6c, light travelling the same way as the observer: q = 0.5. The density falls to 0.25 of its value, the volume doubles, and the energy is \(0.25\times2=0.5\) of what it was.

The tempting mistake: treat the light complex as a body at rest in K and shrink its volume by 1/1.25 = 0.8. That gives \(0.25\times0.8=0.2\), not 0.5. The boundary moves with the light, not with a body at rest in either frame, so the contraction of a material body does not apply to it.
A case that cannot catch the mistake: light crossing the motion at right angles in K has q = 1.25, and 1/q = 0.8 happens to equal the material factor. Test with light along the motion.
The calculation needs no light quanta. The mass-energy paper of September 1905 starts from exactly this transformation of light energy, and does not assume its own conclusion in advance.

margin.text: Here \(u\) is energy density and \(V_{\mathrm{packet}}\) the volume of the complex. The letter \(L\) is avoided: in this paper it names a magnetic component, and in the mass-energy paper the emitted energy. The calculation follows one bounded complex of light; it gives light no rest frame.
